quick: 100 mg once daily (commonly 100-200 mg/day) for UTI/respiratory infection
May be taken with or without food; separate from antacids/minerals by 2 h
Avoid - fluoroquinolones may affect developing cartilage
Reduce dose in renal impairment (renally eliminated)
Tendon/joint symptoms, QT in at-risk patients, blood glucose, CNS effects
summary: Balofloxacin is a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibacterial that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, used (mainly in Japan, Korea and India) for urinary tract infections and other susceptible bacterial infections. It is bactericidal against many Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms. As a fluoroquinolone it shares the class risks of tendinopathy/tendon rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects, peripheral neuropathy and dysglycemia. It is not FDA-approved; this record is based on regional approvals, manufacturer SmPC and the fluoroquinolone class.
indications: Acute uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections caused by susceptible organisms
Respiratory tract infections (e.g. chronic bronchitis exacerbation, pneumonia) caused by susceptible organisms (per regional labeling)
Other susceptible bacterial infections per local approved indications

dosage.n: Per regional labeling; duration by infection
Higher dose for more severe/less susceptible infection

dosage.d: Reduce dose or extend interval per creatinine clearance
Use lowest effective dose; assess renal function

admin: May be taken with or without food
Separate dosing from antacids and products containing magnesium, aluminium, calcium, iron or zinc by at least 2 hours
Maintain adequate hydration to reduce crystalluria risk
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
moa: Balofloxacin inhibits the bacterial enzymes DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, which are essential for DNA replication, transcription, repair and recombination. Inhibition disrupts bacterial DNA supercoiling and chromosome segregation, producing a bactericidal effect against susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to balofloxacin or other quinolones
History of tendon disorders related to fluoroquinolone use
Children and growing adolescents (cartilage toxicity concern)
relative: History of QT prolongation or significant cardiac disease
Epilepsy or conditions predisposing to seizures

preg: Fluoroquinolones, including balofloxacin, are generally avoided in pregnancy because of concern about effects on developing cartilage and joints. Use only if there is no safer alternative and the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
lact: Fluoroquinolones distribute into breast milk and may affect infant cartilage; breastfeeding is generally not recommended during balofloxacin therapy. If treatment is essential, consider temporarily withholding breastfeeding.
renal: Balofloxacin is largely eliminated by the kidneys, so dose reduction or interval extension is required in moderate-to-severe renal impairment. Follow regional/manufacturer dosing guidance and maintain hydration.
hepatic: Use with caution in significant hepatic impairment. Rare hepatotoxicity is a class effect of fluoroquinolones; monitor for signs of liver injury.

major: QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, macrolides) - additive risk of torsades de pointes
Corticosteroids - increased risk of tendon rupture, especially in the elderly
Theophylline - quinolones may raise theophylline levels and seizure risk
moderate: Multivalent cations (antacids, sucralfate, iron, calcium, zinc, dairy) - chelation reduces absorption; separate by >=2 hours
Antidiabetic agents - risk of hypo- or hyperglycemia
NSAIDs - may enhance CNS stimulation/seizure risk
interactions.food: Food may delay absorption modestly; avoid taking with dairy or mineral supplements.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol due to additive CNS effects.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause transient elevations in liver enzymes and disturbances of blood glucose; monitor as indicated.

emergency: Suspected aortic dissection (sudden severe chest/back/abdominal pain)

monitoring: Tendon and joint symptoms - stop the drug if tendon pain or swelling occurs
ECG/QT in patients with cardiac risk factors or on other QT-prolonging drugs
Renal and hepatic function as clinically indicated
counsel: Stop and seek advice if you develop tendon pain/swelling, numbness/tingling, or new mood/CNS symptoms
Take at least 2 hours apart from antacids, dairy, iron, calcium or zinc products
Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sun protection
Diabetics should monitor blood sugar more closely
Complete the full course and report severe or bloody diarrhea
pk: Peak plasma concentration about 1-2 hours after oral dosing
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; balofloxacin is marketed in countries such as Japan, Korea and India - dosing and indications here follow regional SmPC/BNF and the fluoroquinolone class rather than an FDA label

Shares fluoroquinolone class warnings: disabling/potentially irreversible tendinitis and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and QT prolongation - reserve for when alternatives are unsuitable
Chelated by multivalent cations - separate from antacids, iron, calcium, zinc and dairy by at least 2 hours
Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and growing children due to cartilage concerns
Monitor blood glucose in diabetics; both hypo- and hyperglycemia have been reported with fluoroquinolones
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the once-daily schedule. Do not double the dose. Complete the full course to avoid resistance.
overdose: There is limited specific information on balofloxacin overdose. As with other fluoroquinolones, expect exaggerated effects such as nausea, CNS stimulation (including seizures) and possible QT prolongation. There is no specific antidote; treat supportively with cardiac and neurologic monitoring, adequate hydration, and seizure management as needed. Hemodialysis removes only a limited amount.
